Rung during the Freedom Parade of RAF Waddington to mark the 55th anniversary of RAF Waddington being granted the Freedom of the City of Lincoln on 25th April 1959.

The quarter peal was rung whilst 120 personnel from RAF Waddington exercised their right to parade through the City of Lincoln with Colours flying, bayonets fixed and bands playing. The parade was led by the RAF Waddington Pipes and Drums.

The Parade came to a halt at the City War Memorial on the High Street where the official salute was given to the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, Councillor Patrick Vaughan, Her Majesty’s Lord-Lieutenant for the County of Lincolnshire, Mr Tony Worth, the City Sheriff, Mrs Patricia Carter, to members of the City of Lincoln Civic Party and to other City Dignitaries. This was then followed by a fly-past by planes stationed at RAF Waddington and the inspection of the Parade by the Mayor. The Parade then continued on up the High Street passing the Guildhall and finally came to an end at City Hall.

Rung with the bells half muffled in memory of Walter Froggatt whose funeral took place earlier today at Nettleham, Lincs.

Walter was the former Tower Captain here at St Mary-le-Wigford for many years, and it was down to his encouragement and determination that this tower had a thriving band, being the teaching tower for the City. Over the decades Walter taught many young ringers to ring on the four bells in this tower, with many of them ringing their first quarter peal here. His contribution to ringing in the Lincoln area was recognised when he was made an Honorary Life Member of the Lincoln Diocesan Guild back in 2002.
Walter’s memory and legacy will live on with the bells at St Mary-le-Wigford which he so loved.

Specially arranged and rung with the bells half muffled in memory of Walter Froggatt who sadly passed away last week.

Walter was the former Tower Captain here at St Mary-le-Wigford for many years, and it was down to his encouragement and determination that this tower had a thriving band, being the teaching tower for the City. Over the decades Walter taught many young ringers to ring on the four bells in this tower, with many of them ringing their first quarter peal here. His contribution to ringing in the Lincoln area was recognised when he was made an Honorary Life Member of the Lincoln Diocesan Guild back in 2002. Walter’s memory and legacy will live on with the bells at St Mary-le-Wigford which he so loved.

Rung for the Commemoration Service to mark the Centenary of the Great War and to remember Ernest Pitcher VC.
Pitcher, a Swanage resident, was 28 years old, and a petty officer in the Royal Navy during the First World War when the following deed took place for which he was awarded the VC:

On 8 August 1917 in the Bay of Biscay, Atlantic, Petty Officer Pitcher was the 4-inch gun layer on HMS Dunraven (one of the Q ships) when she was shelled by an enemy submarine. He and the rest of the crew waited while the battle went on overhead and all around them. When the magazine below them caught fire they took up cartridges and held them on their knees to prevent the heat of the deck igniting them and when the magazine finally blew up they were all blown into the air. His VC was awarded by ballot of the gun crew.
Ernest Pitcher also received the Distinguished Service Medal, the French Medaille Militaire and the Croix de Guerre.

Specially arranged and rung to commemorate the 70th anniversary of Operation Market Garden 17th – 26th September 1944, in particular the Battle of Arnhem where the First Airborne Divisional Signals tried to secure a bridgehead over the River Rhine, later nicknamed ‘A Bridge too Far'.
Especially remembering the 27 members of the First Airborne Divisional Signals who were billeted at Caythorpe and who did not return from Arnhem.

Caythorpe has close connections to Arnhem. During the Second World War the First Airborne Divisional Signals were based at Caythorpe. To this day Caythorpe maintains close links with 216 Parachute Signal Squadron, who every year hold a Parade and Service on the first Sunday in September ‘Arnhem Sunday’ at this Church, were they have Regimental Memorial Windows and the Arnhem Memorial.
We had intended to ring and name a new method Arnhem, however this proved to be 'A Method too Far!!!'

Specially arranged and rung to mark the 225th anniversary of the bells being cast by Thomas Osborn of Downham Market and officially opened and rung for the first time on 23rd October 1789.
The opening was recorded in the Norwich Journal dated 31st October 1789:

“On Friday last a new peal of six bells were opened at Timberland in the County of Lincoln by a society of ringers from Bicker in the said county with the peals of treble and court bob. After much good ringing on that day the gentlemen in the town and neighbourhood met at the Miller’s Arms where the evening was spent with the greatest harmony and satisfaction. The bells were cast and hung by Thomas Osborn of Downham in Norfolk and are allowed by capital Judges to be a very fine peal of bells.”

Rung with the bells half muffled by the local band in memory of Reverend Canon Bryan Barrodale, acting as Honorary Priest here at All Saints from 2006 after he moved to Branston in retirement from Nottinghamshire, who sadly passed away on 29th September 2014 aged 70.

This quarter was rung immediately prior to his Funeral Service and Requiem Mass held at this Church. Prior to the quarter the death knell was rung in the form of the nine tailors and age being tolled on the ‘Announcing Bell’ here at Branston, the fifth. After the quarter and up to the start of the service whole pull and stand was rung with the tenor tolling.
Immediately after the Service as the coffin, clergy and congregation left a 660 of Doubles was rung consisting of 180 whole pull Plain Hunt on five and 480 of Plain Bob Doubles.
The band wish to associate Joe Spencer, local ringer and long standing friend of Bryan’s, with this quarter.
Our thoughts are with his wife Barbara and the rest of his family at this difficult time. He will be greatly missed by all who knew him, especially his sense of humour.
